item.title: Go Slice Conversion []T to []interface{} Explained with Code Examples
item.description:
“Go Slice Conversion []T to []interface{} Explained with Code Examples”

In Go, you often encounter situations where you need to convert a slice of a specific type, like []string or []int, into a slice of empty interfaces, []interface{}. This is particularly useful when working with functions that expect arguments of type []interface{} or when dealing with collections that need to hold values of mixed types. However, Go does not allow a direct, implicit conversion between []T and []interface{}. Why is this the case, and what are the correct ways to achieve this conversion?

item.title: Go Struct Tags Explained: Usage with Reflection and Common Packages
item.description:
“Go Struct Tags Explained: Usage with Reflection and Common Packages”

In the Go programming language, struct tags are special string literals appended to a field declaration within a struct. They provide a mechanism to attach arbitrary metadata to that field, information that is typically leveraged by external packages or custom logic accessed through the reflect package at runtime.

Core Purpose and Convention of Struct Tags

A struct tag’s primary function is to embed meta-information about how a struct field should be transformed when encoded or decoded into different formats (like JSON, XML, or database records) or how it should be stored/retrieved.

item.title: Go JSON Serialization Accessing Unexported Fields Methods
item.description:
“Go JSON Serialization Accessing Unexported Fields Methods”

How can a developer successfully serialize or deserialize Go struct fields that are intentionally unexported (lowercase) when using the built-in encoding/json package? The standard library’s JSON mechanism typically restricts access to only exported fields.

The Technical Restriction and Solution Path

The core issue stems from how Go’s json package interacts with reflection. It fundamentally cannot view or process unexported fields unless the type being accessed belongs strictly to the same package where the field is defined. When dealing with external packages or API documentation generation, this limitation becomes apparent.
